narrative:
The model estimated a 54.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means it judged failure slightly more likely than passing, so your law school application was denied under a risk-based threshold; this is a probability judgment, not a certainty about your ability.

The strongest factor in the prediction was your Year 3 class-rank decile, 5.00 versus an accepted-student average of 5.79. Although it ranked first in influence, it actually leaned toward a pass. The second most important factor was your LSAT score, 23 compared with an accepted-student average of 37.18, which pushed strongly toward likely bar failure. The third was your undergraduate GPA, 2.30 versus 3.23 for accepted students, which also pushed toward failure. The denial therefore reflects that the LSAT and GPA concerns outweighed the favorable Year 3 signal.

Next, focus on the two clearest levers. Prepare carefully and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, and strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program if feasible. Meet with an admissions adviser, seek schools that review applications holistically, and provide context for your record. Request feedback and consider reapplying after meaningful improvement.
